newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Rate cut not ruled out by German GDP rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Rate cut not ruled out by German GDP rise.

text.p: Germany's economy grew strongly in the third quarter, data showed on Wednesday, but analysts said there was still scope for a possible interest rate cut, further bond market gains and a weaker mark.
Adjusted figures published by the Bundesbank showed that third quarter gross domestic product (GDP) rose by 0.8 percent against the second quarter, when output rose by 1.5 percent.

Year-on-year growth in pan-German GDP accelerated to 1.9 percent from 1.1 percent, according to Bundesbank data which were revised slightly down from numbers released initially by the Federal Statistics Office.
The GDP numbers came in towards the top end of market expectations, initially pushing the mark up a pfennig against the dollar before the German currency eased back.
"The rise...might suggest that the German recovery is now very much on track," HSBC analyst Stephen King wrote in a research note.
But, King added, renewed GDP weakness in the fourth quarter would end up leaving the Bundesbank's bias towards easing rates "firmly in place".

Adolf Rosenstock at the Industrial Bank of Japan, who expects fourth-quarter growth to slow to 0.3 percent, agreed: "This is just a look into the rear-view mirror, and ahead of us seems to be a rather flat fourth quarter."

A jump of 2.9 percent in October industrial orders also brightened a picture clouded on Tuesday by a sharp fall in industrial output in the same month. But analysts still expect November unemployment, due out on Thursday, to rise.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt also said recovery was gaining strength and official forecasts -- of 1.25 percent growth this year and 2.5 percent in 1997 -- could be met.

"There are good prospects for turning the current recovery into a sustained economic upswing," he said. Rexrodt said that stronger third quarter investment was encouraging, but only a sustained increase would cut high German unemployment.
Rosenstock and King said there was still a chance that the Bundesbank would shave its repo rate, which is now at three percent, in the new year.

But Juergen Pfister at Commerzbank ruled out any further rate reductions. "We don't see any possibility for a further cut in short-term interest rates as all the Bundesbank's arguments for lower rates -- a weak economy and a stronger mark -- are no longer there," he said.
The third quarter growth figure may lead to a slight correction in rallying German bond markets, but the market was still well underpinned, said Rob Hayward at Bank of America.

"I think the bund market is well supported and inflation is well under control," Hayward said. The 10-year bund eased 30 basis points after the data and then traded sideways, with the yield up to 5.65 percent.
Pfister said: "We have shifted from a low-growth scenario to a moderate growth scenario, so we expect some change in the bond market -- but in early 1997 rather than sooner."
Economists agreed that the GDP numbers would give a modest boost to the mark, which came off its highs to stand at 1.5615 to the dollar at 1240 GMT from 1.5668 on Tuesday.
But the underlying picture of low interest rates and the prospect of linking up in 1999 with a larger group of weaker currencies in European monetary union (EMU) still pointed to mark weakness.
"EMU remains a risk for the mark," Rosenstock said.
